full_text: Page: 1 4 4 2 RESEARCH PAPER *Author for Correspondence: Dr Raja TK Anti-Rabies Vaccine Compliance, Dog Bite Management Practices, and Cultural Taboos Among Animal Bite Victims Attending an Urban Health Training Centre in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu: A Cross-Sectional Study Dr Prasanth K1, Dr Raja TK2, Dr Keerthana S3, Dr Roshith SJ 4, Dr Saranya T5, Dr Janaarthanan H 6, Dr Bhargava Ram G S7, Dr Siddharthan J 8, Dr Snehaa S 9 and Dr Sharib Kausar 10 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10Post graduate, 2Professor & HOD Department of Community Medicine , Shri Sathya Sai Medical College and Research Institute , Affiliated to Sri Balaji Vidyapeeth ( SBV) (Deemed to be University) , Tamil Nadu , India. Corresponding Author: Dr Raja TK Received: 24th April, 2026; Revised: 20th May 2026; Accepted: 30th June, 2026; Available Online: 10th July, 2026 ABSTRACT Background: Rabies is a fatal zoonotic disease with a 100% case fatality rate once clinical symptoms develop. India bears approximately 36% of global rabies deaths, with dog bites responsible for over 99% of transmission. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) comprising wound management and a complete course of anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) is the only proven prevention after exposure. However, compliance with the full ARV schedule and adherence to correct wound management remain suboptimal in many parts of India. Cultural taboos following dog bites further delay and impede appropriate care-seeking. This study aimed to assess the pattern of dog bites, wound management practices, compliance with the ARV regimen, and prevalent cultural taboos among animal bite victims attending an urban anti-rabies clinic in Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. Methods: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted at the Anti-Rabies Clinic of the Urban Health Training Centre (UHTC), Thiruporur, Chengalpattu district, from February 2025 to April 2025. A total of 301 patients with WHO- defined Category II and III animal bite wounds were recruited by consecutive sampling. Data were collected using a pre- tested, semi-structured questionnaire. Chi-square test and independent samples t-test were used for statistical analysis. Results: The overall ARV completion rate (up to the 3rd dose, the clinically critical threshold in the intradermal regimen) was 70.8%. The most common reason for non-compliance was loss of wages (41.4%), followed by forgotten dates (35.6%) and school timing conflicts (23.0%). Only 5% of participants correctly washed the bite wound with soap and water and applied an antiseptic. Cultural taboos were highly prevalent: 83.4% followed food restrictions after dog bite, with 69.9% avoiding non-vegetarian food. The site of dog bite was significantly associated with ARV compliance (p=0.021), as was the fate of the biting animal (p=0.003). Conclusions: ARV compliance in urban Chengalpattu is moderate (70.8%), and correct wound management is critically low (5%). Prevalent cultural taboos represent a major barrier to appropriate care. Targeted health education, behaviour change communication, and simplified reminder systems are urgently required to improve PEP outcomes in line with India’s National Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) 2030 target. Conflict of interest: None INTRODUCTION Rabies is an acute viral encephalitis caused by the neurotropic RNA virus Lyssavirus, belonging to the family Rhabdoviridae. It is a uniformly fatal zoonotic disease once clinical symptoms appear, with a case fatality rate of virtually 100%.1 The virus is transmitted primarily through the saliva of infected animals, typically via bites that breach the skin. Both domestic and wild animals can serve as reservoirs, but domestic dogs are responsible for more than 99% of human rabies deaths worldwide.2 Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths per year, predominantly in Asia and Africa.3 India accounts for approximately 36% of global rabies deaths Page: 1 4 4 3 Anti-Rabies Vaccine Compliance, Dog Bite Management Practices, and Cultural Taboos Among Animal Bite Victims Attending an Urban Health Training Centre in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu: A Cross-Sectional Study IJDDT, Volume 16 Issue 72s, 2026 and is endemic for the disease. The National Rabies Control Programme (NRCP) reported 6,644 clinically suspected rabies deaths between 2012 and 2022.4 Tamil Nadu has witnessed a particularly alarming surge in recent years: as of October 2024, the state recorded 34 human rabies deaths and 6.42 lakh dog bite cases — the highest in five years — compared to 18 deaths and 4.41 lakh cases in 2023.5 A landmark community-based nationwide cross-sectional survey by Schneider et al. (2025), covering 60 districts across 15 Indian states from 2022 to 2023, provided the most comprehensive recent estimate of the animal bite burden and human rabies deaths in India. This study found that the annual animal bite incidence and the proportion of bite victims receiving a complete ARV course remain far below what is required to achieve the WHO ‘Zero by 30’ target.6 Despite rabies being entirely preventable with timely and correct post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), compliance with the full ARV schedule remains suboptimal across India. The WHO-recommended PEP protocol consists of: (a) immediate and thorough wound washing with soap and water; (b) wound categorisation; and (c) administration of ARV using either the intramuscular (IM) route — Essen regimen (days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28) or Zagreb regimen (days 0, 7, 21) — or the intradermal (ID) route using the updated Thai Red Cross regimen (0.1 mL at two sites on days 0, 3, 7, and 28). Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is additionally required for Category III wounds.3 A mixed-method study from Puducherry (2024) found that the commonest reason for ARV non-compliance was failure to remember the vaccination schedule (52.4%), followed by poor awareness and lack of time.7 A cross- sectional record-based study from Thiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu (2024) — geographically adjacent to Chengalpattu — found an ARV compliance rate of 73.1%, with forgotten dates and distance from the hospital as the main barriers.8 A prospective study from Gujarat (2025) similarly documented that stray dog bites, low education, and wage loss were key predictors of non-compliance.9 Compounding the clinical challenge, cultural taboos and misconceptions about dog bites are widespread in Indian communities. Traditional practices — such as food restrictions, avoidance of bathing, and reliance on native healers — delay definitive medical care and persist despite health education efforts.10 A KAP study from rural Patna (2024) found that even in communities with awareness of rabies, correct wound-washing practices and timely PEP initiation remained alarmingly low.11 India launched its National Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) in 2021, operationalised in 2023, with the goal of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2030 using a One Health approach.12 Achieving this target requires granular, district-level data on ARV compliance, wound management practices, and cultural barriers. There is a paucity of such data from Chengalpattu district specifically. This study was therefore designed to generate evidence to inform targeted interventions in this rapidly urbanising district of Tamil Nadu. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study Design and Setting A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted at the Anti-Rabies Clinic of the Urban Health Training Centre (UHTC), Thiruporur, Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. The UHTC is the urban field practice area of Shri Sathya Sai Medical College & Research Institute (SSSMCRI) and provides healthcare — including maternal and child health, immunisation, NCD management, and anti-rabies services — to a catchment population of approximately 46,674. Study Period The study was conducted from February 2025 to April 2025 (three months). The total study period including planning and analysis was January to May 2025. Sample Size The sample size was calculated using the formula n = Z2 × p(1−p) / d2. Based on a prior urban study reporting ARV compliance of 76.5% (p = 0.765), with 95% confidence level (Z = 1.96) and a margin of error of 5% (d = 0.05), the minimum required sample size was 278. Accounting for a 10% non-response rate, the final target was 306; a total of 301 participants were enrolled. Study Participants and Sampling All patients attending the Anti-Rabies Clinic at UHTC during the study period were considered. Inclusion criteria: permanent residents of Thiruporur with WHO- defined Category II or Category III animal bite wounds, of all ages and both sexes. Exclusion criteria: Category I wounds (no breach of skin integrity); participants who had received their first two ARV doses at another facility; and individuals who declined to provide informed consent. A consecutive sampling method was used to recruit all eligible patients presenting during the study period until the target sample was achieved. Data Collection Data were collected using a pre-tested, semi-structured, interviewer-administered questionnaire in Tamil (the local language). The questionnaire was developed in English, translated into Tamil by a bilingual expert, back-translated for validation, and pre-tested on 20 patients before the main study. The questionnaire comprised four sections: 1. Socio-demographic data: age, sex, religion, education, occupation, type and size of family, and socioeconomic status (modified BG Prasad’s classification, updated 2024). 2. Pattern of dog bite: type of biting animal (pet or stray), immunisation status of the biting animal, fate of the biting animal after the bite, time and place of bite, circumstance of bite (provoked or unprovoked), site of bite on the body, presence of bleeding, and WHO wound categorisation (Category II or III). Page: 1 4 4 4 Anti-Rabies Vaccine Compliance, Dog Bite Management Practices, and Cultural Taboos Among Animal Bite Victims Attending an Urban Health Training Centre in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu: A Cross-Sectional Study IJDDT, Volume 16 Issue 72s, 2026 3. Wound management practices: method of wound washing, agents used, antiseptic application, time lag between bite and wound washing, time interval from bite to first ARV dose, and prior history of dog bite and vaccination. 4. ARV compliance: doses received, dates of each dose, reasons for missed or delayed doses, and completion status. 5. Cultural taboos: food restrictions, advice sources for taboos, and other practices observed after dog bite. Outcome Definitions ARV compliance was defined as receipt of all three doses of the intradermal Thai Red Cross regimen (days 0, 3, and 7) — the minimum clinically essential doses for adequate protective immunity. Corresponding Author: Dr Raja TK Received: 24th April, 2026; Revised: 20th May 2026; Accepted: 30th June, 2026; Available Online: 10th July, 2026 ABSTRACT Background: Rabies is a fatal zoonotic disease with a 100% case fatality rate once clinical symptoms develop. India bears approximately 36% of global rabies deaths, with dog bites responsible for over 99% of transmission. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) comprising wound management and a complete course of anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) is the only proven prevention after exposure. However, compliance with the full ARV schedule and adherence to correct wound management remain suboptimal in many parts of India. Cultural taboos following dog bites further delay and impede appropriate care-seeking. This study aimed to assess the pattern of dog bites, wound management practices, compliance with the ARV regimen, and prevalent cultural taboos among animal bite victims attending an urban anti-rabies clinic in Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. Methods: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted at the Anti-Rabies Clinic of the Urban Health Training Centre (UHTC), Thiruporur, Chengalpattu district, from February 2025 to April 2025. A total of 301 patients with WHO- defined Category II and III animal bite wounds were recruited by consecutive sampling. Data were collected using a pre- tested, semi-structured questionnaire. Chi-square test and independent samples t-test were used for statistical analysis. Results: The overall ARV completion rate (up to the 3rd dose, the clinically critical threshold in the intradermal regimen) was 70.8%. The most common reason for non-compliance was loss of wages (41.4%), followed by forgotten dates (35.6%) and school timing conflicts (23.0%). Only 5% of participants correctly washed the bite wound with soap and water and applied an antiseptic. Cultural taboos were highly prevalent: 83.4% followed food restrictions after dog bite, with 69.9% avoiding non-vegetarian food. The site of dog bite was significantly associated with ARV compliance (p=0.021), as was the fate of the biting animal (p=0.003). Conclusions: ARV compliance in urban Chengalpattu is moderate (70.8%), and correct wound management is critically low (5%). Prevalent cultural taboos represent a major barrier to appropriate care. Targeted health education, behaviour change communication, and simplified reminder systems are urgently required to improve PEP outcomes in line with India’s National Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) 2030 target. Conflict of interest: None INTRODUCTION Rabies is an acute viral encephalitis caused by the neurotropic RNA virus Lyssavirus, belonging to the family Rhabdoviridae. It is a uniformly fatal zoonotic disease once clinical symptoms appear, with a case fatality rate of virtually 100%.1 The virus is transmitted primarily through the saliva of infected animals, typically via bites that breach the skin. Both domestic and wild animals can serve as reservoirs, but domestic dogs are responsible for more than 99% of human rabies deaths worldwide.2 Globally, rabies causes an estimated 59,000 human deaths per year, predominantly in Asia and Africa.3 India accounts for approximately 36% of global rabies deaths Page: 1 4 4 3 Anti-Rabies Vaccine Compliance, Dog Bite Management Practices, and Cultural Taboos Among Animal Bite Victims Attending an Urban Health Training Centre in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu: A Cross-Sectional Study IJDDT, Volume 16 Issue 72s, 2026 and is endemic for the disease. The National Rabies Control Programme (NRCP) reported 6,644 clinically suspected rabies deaths between 2012 and 2022.4 Tamil Nadu has witnessed a particularly alarming surge in recent years: as of October 2024, the state recorded 34 human rabies deaths and 6.42 lakh dog bite cases — the highest in five years — compared to 18 deaths and 4.41 lakh cases in 2023.5 A landmark community-based nationwide cross-sectional survey by Schneider et al. (2025), covering 60 districts across 15 Indian states from 2022 to 2023, provided the most comprehensive recent estimate of the animal bite burden and human rabies deaths in India. This study found that the annual animal bite incidence and the proportion of bite victims receiving a complete ARV course remain far below what is required to achieve the WHO ‘Zero by 30’ target.6 Despite rabies being entirely preventable with timely and correct post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), compliance with the full ARV schedule remains suboptimal across India. The WHO-recommended PEP protocol consists of: (a) immediate and thorough wound washing with soap and water; (b) wound categorisation; and (c) administration of ARV using either the intramuscular (IM) route — Essen regimen (days 0, 3, 7, 14, 28) or Zagreb regimen (days 0, 7, 21) — or the intradermal (ID) route using the updated Thai Red Cross regimen (0.1 mL at two sites on days 0, 3, 7, and 28). Rabies immunoglobulin (RIG) is additionally required for Category III wounds.3 A mixed-method study from Puducherry (2024) found that the commonest reason for ARV non-compliance was failure to remember the vaccination schedule (52.4%), followed by poor awareness and lack of time.7 A cross- sectional record-based study from Thiruvallur district, Tamil Nadu (2024) — geographically adjacent to Chengalpattu — found an ARV compliance rate of 73.1%, with forgotten dates and distance from the hospital as the main barriers.8 A prospective study from Gujarat (2025) similarly documented that stray dog bites, low education, and wage loss were key predictors of non-compliance.9 Compounding the clinical challenge, cultural taboos and misconceptions about dog bites are widespread in Indian communities. Traditional practices — such as food restrictions, avoidance of bathing, and reliance on native healers — delay definitive medical care and persist despite health education efforts.10 A KAP study from rural Patna (2024) found that even in communities with awareness of rabies, correct wound-washing practices and timely PEP initiation remained alarmingly low.11 India launched its National Action Plan for Dog-Mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE) in 2021, operationalised in 2023, with the goal of eliminating dog-mediated human rabies deaths by 2030 using a One Health approach.12 Achieving this target requires granular, district-level data on ARV compliance, wound management practices, and cultural barriers. There is a paucity of such data from Chengalpattu district specifically. This study was therefore designed to generate evidence to inform targeted interventions in this rapidly urbanising district of Tamil Nadu. MATERIALS AND…

analysis.summary_en: This cross-sectional study conducted in Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu, aimed to assess anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) compliance, wound management practices, and cultural taboos among individuals bitten by dogs. The study included 301 participants with WHO-defined Category II and III wounds, recruited via consecutive sampling. Results showed that 70.8% completed the ARV regimen up to the third dose, while only 5% practiced correct wound management. Non-compliance was primarily due to loss of wages, forgotten dates, and school timing conflicts. Cultural taboos, such as food restrictions, were highly prevalent, with 83.4% avoiding non-vegetarian food. The study found that the fate of the biting dog was significantly associated with ARV compliance. However, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the reliance on self-reported data may introduce bias. The findings suggest the need for improved education and support systems to enhance ARV adherence and wound care practices.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估泰米尔纳德邦 Chengalpattu 区城市抗 狂犬病 诊所就诊的动物咬伤受害者的狗咬伤模式、伤口处理做法、抗逆转录病毒疗法的依从性以及普遍的文化禁忌。印度约占全球 狂犬病 死亡人数的 36%,其中 99% 以上是由狗咬伤造成的。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 通过连续采样,总共招募了 301 名 WHO 定义的 II 类和 III 类动物咬伤患者。该研究是在研究期间在泰米尔纳德邦 Chengalpattu 区的一个城市健康培训中心进行的。所需的最低样本量为 278 个,考虑到 10% 的无答复率,调整为 306 个,最终招募了 301 名参与者。
elements_zh.methods: 使用泰米尔语(当地语言)预先测试的半结构化访谈问卷收集数据。使用卡方检验和独立样本t检验进行统计分析。数据输入 Microsoft Excel 2019 并使用 IBM SPSS Statistics 25.0 版进行分析。
elements_zh.main_results: 总体 ARV 完成率为 70.8%(直至第 3 剂,即皮内治疗方案的临床关键阈值)。只有 5% 的参与者正确地用肥皂和水清洗咬伤伤口并使用消毒剂。不遵守规定的最常见原因是工资损失(41.4%),其次是忘记日期(35.6%)和上课时间冲突(23.0%)。狗咬伤的部位与 ARV 依从性显着相关 (p=0.021),咬伤动物的命运也是如此 (p=0.003)。随着后续剂量的增加,依从性逐渐下降:228 名(75.7%)接受了第二剂,213 名(70.8%)完成了第三剂,166 名(55.1%)完成了第四剂。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: Chengalpattu 城市的 ARV 依从性中等(70.8%),而正确的伤口处理则极低(5%)。咬人狗的命运与 ARV 依从性显着相关,表明了解狗的状况可能会影响对 疫苗接种 方案的依从性。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要采取有针对性的干预措施,以提高狗咬伤受害者的抗逆转录病毒药物依从性和伤口处理实践。他们还强调了文化禁忌在形成咬伤后行为中的作用,这可以为解决这些障碍的公共卫生策略提供信息。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的横断面设计限制了其建立因果关系的能力。证据基于自我报告的数据,这可能会引入偏见。由于普遍性的限制和召回偏差的可能性,置信水平为中等。

title_zh: 参加泰米尔纳德邦 Chengalpattu 区城市健康培训中心的动物咬伤受害者的反 狂犬病 疫苗 合规性、狗咬伤管理实践和文化禁忌:一项横断面研究
source_body_en: Page: 1 4 4 2 RESEARCH PAPER *Author for Correspondence: Dr Raja TK Anti-Rabies Vaccine Compliance, Dog Bite Management Practices, and Cultural Taboos Among Animal Bite Victims Attending an Urban Health Training Centre in Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu: A Cross-Sectional Study Dr Prasanth K1, Dr Raja TK2, Dr Keerthana S3, Dr Roshith SJ 4, Dr Saranya T5, Dr Janaarthanan H 6, Dr Bhargava Ram G S7, Dr Siddharthan J 8, Dr Snehaa S 9 and Dr Sharib Kausar 10 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10Post graduate, 2Professor & HOD Department of Community Medicine , Shri Sathya Sai Medical College and Research Institute , Affiliated to Sri Balaji Vidyapeeth ( SBV) (Deemed to be University) , Tamil Nadu , India. This study aimed to assess the pattern of dog bites, wound management practices, compliance with the ARV regimen, and prevalent cultural taboos among animal bite victims attending an urban anti-rabies clinic in Chengalpattu district, Tamil Nadu. Methods: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted at the Anti-Rabies Clinic of the Urban Health Training Centre (UHTC), Thiruporur, Chengalpattu district, from February 2025 to April 2025. Results: The overall ARV completion rate (up to the 3rd dose, the clinically critical threshold in the intradermal regimen) was 70.8%. India bears approximately 36% of global rabies deaths, with dog bites responsible for over 99% of transmission. Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) comprising wound management and a complete course of anti-rabies vaccine (ARV) is the only proven prevention after exposure. However, compliance with the full ARV schedule and adherence to correct wound management remain suboptimal in many parts of India. Cultural taboos following dog bites further delay and impede appropriate care-seeking. A total of 301 patients with...

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在评估泰米尔纳德邦 Chengalpattu 区城市抗 狂犬病 诊所就诊的动物咬伤受害者的狗咬伤模式、伤口处理做法、抗逆转录病毒疗法的依从性以及普遍的文化禁忌。印度约占全球 狂犬病 死亡人数的 36%,其中 99% 以上是由狗咬伤造成的。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 通过连续采样,总共招募了 301 名 WHO 定义的 II 类和 III 类动物咬伤患者。该研究是在研究期间在泰米尔纳德邦 Chengalpattu 区的一个城市健康培训中心进行的。所需的最低样本量为 278 个,考虑到 10% 的无答复率,调整为 306 个,最终招募了 301 名参与者。
analysis_zh.methods: 使用泰米尔语(当地语言)预先测试的半结构化访谈问卷收集数据。使用卡方检验和独立样本t检验进行统计分析。数据输入 Microsoft Excel 2019 并使用 IBM SPSS Statistics 25.0 版进行分析。
analysis_zh.main_results: 总体 ARV 完成率为 70.8%(直至第 3 剂,即皮内治疗方案的临床关键阈值)。只有 5% 的参与者正确地用肥皂和水清洗咬伤伤口并使用消毒剂。不遵守规定的最常见原因是工资损失(41.4%),其次是忘记日期(35.6%)和上课时间冲突(23.0%)。狗咬伤的部位与 ARV 依从性显着相关 (p=0.021),咬伤动物的命运也是如此 (p=0.003)。随着后续剂量的增加,依从性逐渐下降:228 名(75.7%)接受了第二剂,213 名(70.8%)完成了第三剂,166 名(55.1%)完成了第四剂。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: Chengalpattu 城市的 ARV 依从性中等(70.8%),而正确的伤口处理则极低(5%)。咬人狗的命运与 ARV 依从性显着相关,表明了解狗的状况可能会影响对 疫苗接种 方案的依从性。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果强调需要采取有针对性的干预措施,以提高狗咬伤受害者的抗逆转录病毒药物依从性和伤口处理实践。他们还强调了文化禁忌在形成咬伤后行为中的作用,这可以为解决这些障碍的公共卫生策略提供信息。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究的横断面设计限制了其建立因果关系的能力。证据基于自我报告的数据,这可能会引入偏见。由于普遍性的限制和召回偏差的可能性,置信水平为中等。

title: Health and care workforce-driven transformations can improve workforce stability and strengthen health system resilience

source_records.title: Health and care workforce-driven transformations can improve workforce stability and strengthen health system resilience
Health and care workforce-driven transformations can improve workforce stability and strengthen health system resilience

full_text: Conclusions and policy directionsThe health and care workforce policy-crisis calls for radical transformations in health policy and systems, moving the debate towards capacities and workforce-driven innovation. Four major strategic policy shifts are indicative to fully enhance and integrate the transformative workforce capacities.Establishing a multi-level participatory governance architecture that connects bottom-up capacities and self-efficacy of frontline workers with top-down strategic guidance, using existing knowledge and actionable policy solutions more coherently and effectively.Shifting health systems and the organization of care towards community- and primary care-centred approaches that are better able to stimulate bottom-up innovation and integrate workforce-driven knowledge strategically into wider health policy.Shifting workforce policy from technical approaches on human resources as part of infrastructures towards health and care workers as persons and the workforce as an essential pillar of health systems security and resilience.Improving data and research on workforce-driven innovation to create governance architectures capable of integrating transformative capacities, while ensuring regulation and strategic oversight of workforce stability and health system resilience. IntroductionChanging population health and new security threats require a resilient health and care workforce, yet health workers are exhausted, labour market capacities are decreasing, and a coherent workforce strategy is still lacking in most European countries. In this situation, workforce-driven stability and resilience may emerge bottom-up. However, these capacities are not well understood by health policy. Instead, health and care workers are mostly perceived as critical infrastructure and as a cost factor for health systems, obscuring the view of both the needs of individual health workers and their active role in health systems.This Viewpoint argues that the transformational capacities of the health and care workforce not only need greater attention but also require a new mindset of workforce policy. Bottom-up workforce-driven transformations are crucial for innovating health systems, supporting the implementation of policy reform and advancing equity and inclusiveness in the workforce itself and in healthcare provision. They can strengthen workforce stability, health system resilience and trust in governments and create co-benefits for other sectors. To unlock these capacities, workforce policies must shift from short-term technical crisis solutions towards a coherent strategy that looks beyond headcounts and acknowledges, in a comprehensive and intersectional way, the person behind every health worker, recognizing in most cases a woman and often a migrant.By focusing on the workforce as an active player and an important pillar of health systems, this Viewpoint highlights new capacities for workforce stability and health systems resilience, calling for policy shifts from crisis towards capacities and implementation [1–3]. The Viewpoint introduces changes driven by knowledge and experience of frontline workers, highlights transformational effects in health systems, and explores supportive governance structures for these capacities to flourish. Health and care workforce as an active stakeholder and innovator of health systemsWorkforce-driven capacities are highly flexible, and the transformative effects in health systems are diverse and context-dependent. Five major transformational roles can be identified, although these may not be exclusive.Policy implementersPrimary care workforce reforms in Denmark and Finland illustrate that health workers’ perceptions matter for implementation. Stakeholder inclusion at an early stage of reform can reduce resistance and support the building of a sustainable primary health care workforce [4]. On the other hand, perceived misalignment with the realities of frontline workers may cause demoralization and potentially worsen shortages if health policy does not respond to the concerns [5].System transformersCommunity health workers provide an example of comprehensive bottom-up transformations towards stronger community-centred and primary healthcare supporting vulnerable populations; for example, maternity care for migrant women and children, HIV/AIDS prevention, or support for victims of violence including sexual violence [6].Workforce stabilizersHealth workers seek to adapt and transform their working routines to respond to growing pressures, improving self-efficacy to protect their mental health and prevent stress and burnout as one of the root causes of the workforce crisis [7]. These emerging ad hoc bottom-up capacities for workforce stability were observed, for instance, among general practitioners in Ireland [8] and globally during the coronavirus disease COVID-19 pandemic.Organizational bridge-buildersHealth frontline workers can act at the meso-level of health systems, connecting different professional groups and provider organizations, including public and private sectors. These capacities are particularly important in team-based provider settings and at the crossroads of healthcare and administrative or technical provider groups, such as procurement [9].Social inclusion facilitatorsCapacities for social inclusion, equity and gender equality may emerge from new professional groups and organizational settings, such as community care workers [6], nurse-led primary care for refugees in Germany [10], or intercultural care workers in Czechia improving access to healthcare for Ukraine refugees after Russia’s full-scale invasion [11].Workforce-driven innovations stretch beyond short-term effects of mitigating shortages and facilitating policy implementation and provider management. Health and care workers can mobilize self-efficacy [12] and self-governing capacities to actively design and implement innovations in health systems. Transformative powers are strongest if diverse capacities converge and create a hub of innovation, as illustrated by community health workers strengthening community-centred policy approaches, social inclusion and gender equality [6], or nurse-led care strengthening task shifting, primary health care, new organizational models and access to care for vulnerable groups [10]. Policy implementersPrimary care workforce reforms in Denmark and Finland illustrate that health workers’ perceptions matter for implementation. Stakeholder inclusion at an early stage of reform can reduce resistance and support the building of a sustainable primary health care workforce [4]. On the other hand, perceived misalignment with the realities of frontline workers may cause demoralization and potentially worsen shortages if health policy does not respond to the concerns [5]. System transformersCommunity health workers provide an example of comprehensive bottom-up transformations towards stronger community-centred and primary healthcare supporting vulnerable populations; for example, maternity care for migrant women and children, HIV/AIDS prevention, or support for victims of violence including sexual violence [6]. Workforce stabilizersHealth workers seek to adapt and transform their working routines to respond to growing pressures, improving self-efficacy to protect their mental health and prevent stress and burnout as one of the root causes of the workforce crisis [7]. These emerging ad hoc bottom-up capacities for workforce stability were observed, for instance, among general practitioners in Ireland [8] and globally during the coronavirus disease COVID-19 pandemic. Organizational bridge-buildersHealth frontline workers can act at the meso-level of health systems, connecting different professional groups and provider organizations, including public and private sectors. These capacities are particularly important in team-based provider settings and at the crossroads of healthcare and administrative or technical provider groups, such as procurement [9]. Social inclusion facilitatorsCapacities for social inclusion, equity and gender equality may emerge from new professional groups and organizational settings, such as community care workers [6], nurse-led primary care for refugees in Germany [10], or intercultural care workers in Czechia improving access to healthcare for Ukraine refugees after Russia’s full-scale invasion [11].Workforce-driven innovations stretch beyond short-term effects of mitigating shortages and facilitating policy implementation and provider management. Health and care workers can mobilize self-efficacy [12] and self-governing capacities to actively design and implement innovations in health systems. Transformative powers are strongest if diverse capacities converge and create a hub of innovation, as illustrated by community health workers strengthening community-centred policy approaches, social inclusion and gender equality [6], or nurse-led care strengthening task shifting, primary health care, new organizational models and access to care for vulnerable groups [10]. Translating workforce capacities into health system resilienceHealth and care workers can ensure workforce stability and support resilient health systems in complex ways, but they cannot do the job of governments. Health policy must create governance architectures that are capable of stimulating and supporting workforce-driven actions and integrating transformational capacities strategically into health policy agendas to achieve the desired outcomes. Governance research and theories [13] offer a broader framework for assessing the connections between bottom-up and top-down capacities and their effects, while meso-level approaches specify transformations in health system contexts.Research into professions, for instance, shows that governments in the past have used and nurtured the capacities of high-level professions strategically, mostly medicine, but hampered others [14]. Medical professions are integrated in European health systems, serving as mediators between the state and the citizens, policy implementors and service organizers. These capacities are strongest in social health insurance systems that assigned statutory rights to medical professions, but also matter in national health services and mixed systems. However, elitist profession-based policies may reinforce the workforce crisis, for instance, if the medical profession hampers integrated skill-mix policies, teamwork, or new roles for qualified nurses.Street-level bureaucracy, with its focus on frontline workers and bottom-up innovation, offers a broader approach. It places the linkage of upward (bureaucracy) and downward (street level) dynamics in a wider governance architecture and draws on available practical solutions that support realist and actionable policies, including sensitivity for political instability and vulnerabilities [12, 15]. This research can identify adverse effects, for instance, if workers perform tasks for which they are not sufficiently educated and qualified, as well as conditions for effective bottom-up transformations and innovations, highlighting the importance of strong regulatory frameworks for education and practice.Migrant and refugee health workers in European health systems provide an example of how bottom-up emerging capacities may be used strategically and integrated in stable governance settings, moving beyond an over-simplicist either–or approach on benefits. Romania, for instance, scaled-up investment in medical education and was able to increase the number of international students, generating revenue, improving the quality and competitiveness of education, expanding labour market capacities and creating a new recruitment pool.Transformational capacities may also flourish ad hoc in uncertain political contexts with vulnerable or collapsed infrastructures. Empirical evidence is mostly taken from countries in the Global South [12, 15], yet increasingly relevant in Europe, as most clearly observed in Ukraine after Russia’s full-scale invasion: strong increases in demand for health workers and new competencies intersect with severe decreases, especially in combat regions and specialized professions [16]. In this situation, Ukraine’s healthcare provision, usually defined by governance frameworks and infrastructures, increasingly shifts towards volatile and hybrid models built on bottom-up workforce driven solutions. For instance, nurses take over coordination and mental health physicians rehabilitation tasks; infectious diseases from the past, such as rabies, recur, and animal health issues spill over into the health system, challenging existing prevention tools; and new digital technologies and platforms are used to support psychosocial care and mental health resilience.All these tasks require high flexibility and new knowledge for which the health and care workers are not sufficiently educated and trained. Ukraine illustrates how workforce-driven capacities ensure healthcare provision under conditions of vulnerable governance and infrastructures. Yet, it also highlights lessons to be learned for improving preparedness and protection of the workforce, and strengthening public health [16, 17] and health security [18]. Governments in Europe and beyond should urgently learn these lessons.

title_original: Health and care workforce-driven transformations can improve workforce stability and strengthen health system resilience

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for a resilient health and care workforce to meet changing population health demands and new security threats, highlighting the lack of a coherent workforce strategy in most European countries.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study is a Viewpoint analyzing policy and system-level transformations in health and care workforce strategies, focusing on European countries and their health systems.
analysis.methods: The methods involve examining policy shifts, workforce capacities, and strategic governance architectures through case studies and examples of community health workers, nurse-led care, and other frontline initiatives.
analysis.main_results: The study identifies five major transformational roles of the health and care workforce, including policy implementers, system transformers, workforce stabilizers, social inclusion facilitators, and workforce-driven innovators, with examples from Denmark, Finland, Germany, and Czechia.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that recognizing the health and care workforce as an active player and essential pillar of health systems can lead to new capacities for stability and resilience, offering a novel perspective on workforce policy.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that shifting workforce policy to focus on capacities and integration can improve health system resilience, support policy implementation, and enhance equity and inclusiveness in healthcare provision.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a Viewpoint, which may lack empirical data, and the study does not provide quantitative results, limiting the strength of the conclusions to a moderate level.

analysis.summary_en: This Viewpoint argues that health and care workforce-driven transformations are essential for improving workforce stability and strengthening health system resilience. It highlights the need for a shift from viewing health workers as mere infrastructure to recognizing their active role in policy implementation and system innovation. The study identifies five transformational roles, including policy implementers, system transformers, and social inclusion facilitators, with examples from various European countries. It emphasizes the importance of integrating these capacities into health policy agendas to address the workforce crisis and enhance preparedness. However, the evidence is based on a policy analysis rather than empirical data, limiting the strength of the conclusions to a moderate level.

elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究是一个观点,分析卫生和护理劳动力战略的政策和系统层面的转变,重点关注欧洲国家及其卫生系统。
elements_zh.methods: 这些方法包括通过案例研究和社区卫生工作者、护士主导的护理和其他一线举措的例子来检查政策转变、劳动力能力和战略治理架构。
elements_zh.main_results: 该研究以丹麦、芬兰、德国和捷克为例,确定了卫生和护理劳动力的五个主要转型角色,包括政策实施者、系统变革者、劳动力稳定者、社会包容促进者和劳动力驱动的创新者。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,认识到卫生和护理劳动力是卫生系统的积极参与者和重要支柱,可以带来新的稳定性和复原力能力,为劳动力政策提供新的视角。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,将劳动力政策转向关注能力和一体化可以提高卫生系统的弹性,支持政策实施,并增强医疗保健提供的公平性和包容性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 证据基于观点,可能缺乏经验数据,并且研究没有提供定量结果,将结论的强度限制在中等水平。

analysis_en.research_question_and_background: The study addresses the need for a resilient health and care workforce to meet changing population health demands and new security threats, highlighting the lack of a coherent workforce strategy in most European countries.
analysis_en.study_design_and_population: The study is a Viewpoint analyzing policy and system-level transformations in health and care workforce strategies, focusing on European countries and their health systems.
analysis_en.methods: The methods involve examining policy shifts, workforce capacities, and strategic governance architectures through case studies and examples of community health workers, nurse-led care, and other frontline initiatives.
analysis_en.main_results: The study identifies five major transformational roles of the health and care workforce, including policy implementers, system transformers, workforce stabilizers, social inclusion facilitators, and workforce-driven innovators, with examples from Denmark, Finland, Germany, and Czechia.
analysis_en.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that recognizing the health and care workforce as an active player and essential pillar of health systems can lead to new capacities for stability and resilience, offering a novel perspective on workforce policy.
analysis_en.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that shifting workforce policy to focus on capacities and integration can improve health system resilience, support policy implementation, and enhance equity and inclusiveness in healthcare provision.
analysis_en.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a Viewpoint, which may lack empirical data, and the study does not provide quantitative results, limiting the strength of the conclusions to a moderate level.

title_zh: 卫生和护理劳动力驱动的转型可以提高劳动力稳定性并增强卫生系统的弹性
source_body_en: Conclusions and policy directionsThe health and care workforce policy-crisis calls for radical transformations in health policy and systems, moving the debate towards capacities and workforce-driven innovation. Four major strategic policy shifts are indicative to fully enhance and integrate the transformative workforce capacities.Establishing a multi-level participatory governance architecture that connects bottom-up capacities and self-efficacy of frontline workers with top-down strategic guidance, using existing knowledge and actionable policy solutions more coherently and effectively.Shifting health systems and the organization of care towards community- and primary care-centred approaches that are better able to stimulate bottom-up innovation and integrate workforce-driven knowledge strategically into wider health policy.Shifting workforce policy from technical approaches on human resources as part of infrastructures towards health and care workers as persons and the workforce as an essential pillar of health systems security and resilience.Improving data and research on workforce-driven innovation to create governance architectures capable of integrating transformative capacities, while ensuring regulation and strategic oversight of workforce stability and health system resilience. IntroductionChanging population health and new security threats require a resilient health and care workforce, yet health workers are exhausted, labour market capacities are decreasing, and a coherent workforce strategy is still lacking in most European countries. In this situation, workforce-driven stability and resilience may emerge bottom-up. However, these capacities are not well understood by health policy. abstract_zh: 结论与政策方向健康和护理工作队伍政策危机要求对健康政策和体系进行根本性转变,将讨论重点转向能力和以工作队伍为中心的创新。四个主要的战略政策转变对于充分增强和整合变革性工作队伍能力具有指示意义。建立一个多层级的参与式治理架构,将一线工作人员的自下而上的能力和自信心与自上而下的战略指导相连接,更加协调和有效地利用现有知识和可操作的政策解决方案。将卫生体系和护理组织转向以社区和初级卫生保健为中心的方法,这些方法能够更好地激发自下而上的创新,并将以工作队伍驱动的知识战略性地整合到更广泛的卫生政策中。将工作队伍政策从以人力资源作为基础设施的技术方法,转向将卫生和护理工作人员视为个体,以及将工作队伍视为卫生体系安全和韧性的关键支柱。通过改善关于以工作队伍驱动的创新的数据和研究,创建能够整合变革性能力的治理架构,同时确保对工作队伍稳定性和卫生体系韧性的监管和战略监督。引言变化的人口健康状况和新的安全威胁要求一个有韧性的卫生和护理工作队伍,然而卫生工作者正面临疲惫,劳动力市场能力正在下降,大多数欧洲国家仍缺乏连贯的工作队伍战略。在这种情况下,以工作队伍驱动的稳定性和韧性可能会自下而上产生。然而,这些能力尚未被卫生政策充分理解。相反,卫生和护理工作人员大多被视为关键基础设施的一部分,而未被充分认识到其作为个体和工作队伍在卫生体系中的核心作用。
